meta.title: Who really said “Our host certainly is outspoken” — “Outspoken by whom?” | Quotle.info
meta.description: Neither Ann Landers nor Dorothy Parker. The retort was in the New York Times in 1901, and in Punch in 1934 — before Parker was credited with it in 1944.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Our Host Certainly Is Outspoken" "Outspoken By Whom?'?
meta.ogDescription: A stock gag, not a bon mot. Quote Investigator traces it to 1901; the Dorothy Parker credit appears in 1944 and Ann Landers used it in 1969.

answer.label: Not Ann Landers — an old joke with no author
answer.authorName: Unknown — a stock joke in print by 1901
answer.authorDates: In circulation by 1901 · creator never identified
answer.sourceLine: This is a formula joke, not a line someone coined at a party. Quote Investigator ↗ finds it in the New York Times in 1901, where a henpecked husband told his wife is “outspoken” replies “By whom?” It recurs in a Sally’s Sallies comic strip in 1929 and in Punch in 1934, always with a different target. The Dorothy Parker version — aimed at a hostess — first appears in a Bennett Cerf collection in 1944, and QI’s verdict is careful: “Dorothy Parker may have uttered the witticism, but it was in circulation before she was famous for being clever.” Ann Landers used it in her column in 1969.

source.excerpt: Minnick—Well, there was one thing I remarked about your wife the first time I saw her; she was undoubtedly outspoken. Henpeck—You don’t say! By whom?
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ gives the earliest instance as a New York Times item of 1901, in which a henpecked husband answers “By whom?” on being told his wife is outspoken.

The gag then recurs with its target swapped: a Sally’s Sallies comic strip in 1929 (“Uncle Joe says women are outspoken—by whom?”), Punch in 1934 (“the modern woman is outspoken. By whom?”) and the Hartford Courant in 1937, citing Pearson’s Weekly.
The Dorothy Parker version enters the record in 1944, in a Bennett Cerf collection, with a hostess as the target — forty-three years after the Times printed it.

QI declines to credit Parker outright, writing that she “may have uttered the witticism, but it was in circulation before she was famous for being clever.” That is a statement about who could have said it, not who invented it.
Ann Landers’s turn comes in 1969, when QI records her answering a letter in her column with “Outspoken? By whom?” — using the joke, not making it.
source.excerptNote: Quote Investigator’s transcription of the 1901 New York Times item, the earliest appearance it could find — see the chronology ↗. The joke’s target moves across the later citations (a wife, “women,” “the modern woman,” a hostess), which is the signature of a stock gag rather than a remembered remark.
source.rightsNote: The joke has no identified author and survives as an evolving formula rather than a fixed text, so quotle.info asserts no rights status. The wordings quoted here are short excerpts from the periodicals in Quote Investigator’s chronology.

author.name: Ann Landers
author.heading: About Ann Landers
author.metaLine: Pen name, created 1943 · American newspaper advice column
author.bio: Ann Landers was never one person. The pen name was created by the Chicago Sun-Times columnist Ruth Crowley in 1943 and taken over by Esther “Eppie” Lederer in 1955, who wrote it until 2002. A column answering letters every day needs a reliable supply of snap retorts, and the ones it reached for were usually old. That is why so many stock jokes now carry her byline: she used them in public, under a famous name, in print.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: A joke this portable collects owners. Both of the famous ones arrive long after it was already in print.

items.why: QI places her use at 1969, answering a letter with the same retort — sixty-eight years after the New York Times printed the same retort. See the chronology ↗.

First attached to her in a Bennett Cerf collection of 1944. QI’s wording is deliberately cautious: she “may have uttered the witticism, but it was in circulation before she was famous for being clever.” Repeating a joke well is not the same as writing it.

The target changes every time — a wife in 1901, “women” in 1929, “the modern woman” in 1934, a hostess in 1944. A fixed punchline with a floating target is a formula, and formulas do not have authors.

misattribution.truthLine: The retort was a stock newspaper gag for forty years before anyone thought to put a name on it. Parker may well have used it; so did Ann Landers; neither of them invented it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke turns on a pun that only works in English: “outspoken” looks like a comparative — out-spoken, the way one might be outrun or outvoted — and the retort pretends to read it that way. Its earliest targets are all women described as too talkative, which dates it as precisely as a hemline.

That is also why it migrated so easily. Swap the wife for a hostess and it becomes a Dorothy Parker story; swap the hostess for a letter-writer and it becomes an Ann Landers put-down. The mechanism survives every change of target, which is exactly what lets it keep finding new authors.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator’s hedge on Parker is worth reading carefully, because it is the honest shape of most quotation research. The claim is not that she never said it — a stock joke is precisely the kind of thing a professional wit would deploy. The claim is that the joke existed first, so her saying it tells us nothing about where it came from. Fame works as a magnet in both directions: it attracts jokes that need an author, and it makes anything the famous person repeats sound original.
context.pull: Dorothy Parker may have uttered the witticism, but it was in circulation before she was famous for being clever.
